issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s genuine and reasonable need for premises, rather than a mere desire to use them, can support eviction when the premises are needed to conduct a business and improve inadequate means of support.
material_facts: The owners sought possession to run a hotel business themselves because their existing business had become dull and produced too little income to maintain them adequately.
Witnesses supported the owners’ stated intention and limited income, and that evidence was not materially shaken in cross-examination or rebuttal.
The tenants had originally taken the premises for a limited lease term but remained in possession for many years afterward.
issues.conclusion: The owners proved a genuine, reasonable, and pressing requirement for the premises; the lower courts wrongly treated that requirement as only a desire.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(1)(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 requires an element of need, not merely a wish, but the terms “reasonable requirement” must not be interpreted so narrowly that a genuine need becomes impossible to establish. The principal test is whether the premises are needed for the landlord’s own use or occupation. The Court applied Phiroze Ramanji Desai v. Chandrakant N. Patel and approved B. Balaiah v. Chandoor Lachaiah.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and landlord_needs_premises_for_own_business and existing_income_is_inadequate and need_is_genuine_and_reasonable

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.landlord_needs_premises_for_own_business: The landlord intended to use the premises to conduct the landlord’s own business.
predicates.existing_income_is_inadequate: The landlord’s existing income was insufficient to maintain the landlord adequately.
predicates.need_is_genuine_and_reasonable: Evidence showed that the landlord’s need to use the premises was genuine and reasonable, rather than a mere wish.

issues.definition: When a landlord in an eviction proceeding genuinely and reasonably needs premises for the landlord’s own business because existing income is inadequate, the landlord has established a ground for eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s own occupation of premises includes using them to conduct a business and does not require the landlord to reside there physically.
material_facts: The owners sought to take possession of the premises to run a hotel business themselves.
The lower courts treated the proposed commercial use as outside the meaning of the owners’ own occupation.
The owners were the owners of the premises and sought possession for their own use.
issues.conclusion: Using the premises to run a hotel would constitute the owners’ own occupation, even if they did not physically reside there.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(1)(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 covers a landlord’s occupation for business as well as residence. “Occupation” is not confined to the landlord’s personal physical residence; it can include business use and the needs of persons living with the landlord as members of the same family. The provision must be construed to advance its object of protecting the landlord’s interest where its conditions are met.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.landlord_seeks_personal_use: The landlord sought possession for the landlord’s own use rather than for an unrelated person’s use.
predicates.proposed_use_is_landlord_business: The landlord intended to conduct the landlord’s own business in the premises.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction proceeding, a landlord’s proposed use of premises for the landlord’s own business qualifies as the landlord’s own occupation.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding comparative hardship in an eviction proceeding must assess the relevant advantages and disadvantages of both parties, and the tenant’s displacement alone does not defeat eviction where the landlord’s hardship is greater.
material_facts: The owners’ income was inadequate, and they had no other means to augment it apart from using their premises for a hotel business.

The tenants relied on the hotel as their source of income and showed difficulty finding a comparable building in the same locality, but did not establish that alternative business premises were unavailable elsewhere.
The tenants had occupied the premises for many years beyond the original lease term.
The lower courts did not adequately weigh the owners’ hardship against the tenants’ evidence of hardship.
issues.conclusion: The owners’ hardship from refusal of possession substantially outweighed the tenants’ hardship from eviction, so the comparative balance favoured the owners.
issues.legal_principle: Under the explanation to section 11(1)(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, the court must consider the comparative advantage or disadvantage to landlord and tenant. Each party must adduce evidence of the hardship that granting or refusing eviction would cause; the entire burden cannot be placed on the landlord to prove that the tenant’s hardship is lesser or remediable. Displacement of the tenant, by itself, is not a sufficient reason to refuse eviction. The Court relied on M/s Central Tobacco Co. v. Chandra Prakash, Phiroze Ramanji Desai v. Chandrakant N. Patel, Kelley v. Goodwin, and K. Parasuramaiah v. Pokuri Lakshmamma.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.both_parties_present_hardship_evidence: The landlord and the tenant each adduced evidence about the hardship that granting or refusing eviction would cause.
predicates.landlord_hardship_exceeds_tenant_hardshi: The evidence showed that refusal of possession would cause the landlord greater hardship than eviction would cause the tenant.

issues.definition: When both parties provide hardship evidence in an eviction proceeding and the landlord’s hardship is greater, the comparative balance favours eviction.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may examine the merits despite concurrent factual findings when the lower courts have committed a substantial legal error that misapplies the governing law and risks grave injustice.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both dismissed the owners’ eviction claim.
The lower courts misinterpreted the meaning of reasonable requirement and own occupation and failed to consider material evidence supporting the owners’ need.
The owners appealed by special leave, and the Supreme Court found that the legal misdirection had led to substantial injustice.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court examined the merits and set aside the lower courts’ decisions because their substantial legal error warranted interference despite concurrent findings.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact, it may do so in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 where the lower courts have made a substantial and patent error of law, misapplied the law, overlooked essential evidence, and thereby risked grave and substantial injustice.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_findings and substantial_legal_error and material_evidence_overlooked and grave_injustice_risked

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: A party brought a special leave appeal challenging concurrent decisions of lower courts.
predicates.substantial_legal_error: The lower courts made a substantial legal error in interpreting or applying the governing law.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The lower courts failed to consider evidence essential to deciding the dispute.
predicates.grave_injustice_risked: The legal error and omission of evidence risked causing grave and substantial injustice.

issues.definition: In a special leave appeal from concurrent decisions, a substantial legal error combined with overlooked material evidence and a risk of grave injustice permits the Supreme Court to reexamine the merits.
